Title: A Short History of Financial Euphoria
Author: John Kenneth Galbraith
My Review:
Periods of financial euphoria impair our ability to think rationally. The collective wisdom of the crowd can quickly become collective delusion, drawing entire societies into speculative manias. The error becomes apparent only in hindsight.

While the catalysts for market exuberance differ from one episode to another, a study of enough episodes reveals a patterns. As the market cliché goes, history does not repeat itself, but it often rhymes. The brevity of the public’s memory of such events leaves each generation vulnerable to believing that old rules no longer apply. The value of hindsight is not merely to understand past mistakes but to develop the foresight to recognize them when they begin to reappear.

The lesson is not that investors should become excessively risk-averse. Risk-taking remains an essential part of investing. Rather, Galbraith argues for caution precisely when caution is least fashionable. The goal, then, is to keep extreme greed and extreme fear at arm’s length.

Although this book was published in 1990, its insights remain relevant. Reading it today, one cannot help but wonder what Galbraith would have thought of the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s and early 2000s, and the global financial crisis of 2008.

Title: Educated
Author: Tara Westover
My Review:
On the surface, Tara Westover’s memoir is about breaking out of the mould that her family set for her and defying the strong gravitational pull of her lack of early formal education to attend Harvard and ultimately earn a PhD in History at Cambridge. At its core, however, it is about control, family loyalty, as well as the damaging effects of religious extremism, physical abuse, mental illness, and paranoia.

Westover’s writing is smooth and flows well. It is easy to forget that it is a memoir and not a novel. Her descriptions are raw, vivid, and unforgiving. At times, I regret reminding myself that it is not fictional.

Westover has a talent for reconstructing mental pitfalls. As she recalled details and conversations from a particular past event, I found myself falling into the same pattern of wishful thinking as she did, only to have the rug pulled out from under me. It was obvious in hindsight. The same passage that initially filled me with hope now reveals the cruelty underlying it.

What stood out to me the most was Westover’s depiction of ignorance. How one could be ignorant about being ignorant. How religion could inadvertently facilitate and vindicate ignorance. How you can have so much built upon your ignorant ideals that enlightenment becomes so immensely costly that it is arguably better to remain ignorant. Truth, it seems, has always been at arm’s length for her. Truth is multidimensional, and she has only been able to observe it from a fixed viewpoint through tainted lens. Can conjectures from partial truths remain truths? By taking a sideways step, the illusion is shattered. I imagine that moment to be when she first attended school at 17. As she continues to circle it, gaining perspective, she has shattered more than just her ignorance.

Title: Klara and the Sun
Author: Kazuo Ishiguro
My Review:
In Klara and the Sun, an artificial friend with a deep curiosity for human affairs reminisces about her days with her human child, Josie, and her family. Although designed to cure loneliness, Klara may have been purchased for more than just companionship.

At the current rate of artificial intelligence advancement, the gap between fiction and reality narrows to the extent that it might eventually disqualify this title from the "dystopian" genre. The novel gives the reader a glimpse into a possible near future and the role artificial intelligence could play in our lives.

Through Ishiguro's brilliance, the world gets painted stroke by stroke through the lens of Klara who learns about the world and its main inhabitants with a childlike wonder. Possessing human-like intelligence but different physical capabilities and restraints, Klara's journey raises difficult questions: What does it mean to love? What defines a human soul? And what makes human intelligence unique? This book may very well change your answers to these questions.

Title: Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI
Author: Ethan Mollick
My Review:
Whether you believe AI will soon come to dominate the world and end human supremacy, or remain simply a tool for inventing dad jokes, it has already been freed from its lamp and holds the potential to impact all of our lives to varying degrees.

The recent advancements in generative artificial intelligence have me concerned about how it will affect me personally as I enter the workforce—especially since my interests lie in the fast-paced, ever-changing tech world. Fear motivates change, and change is best approached with a well-informed mind. To accept or to reject; to cling to the past or to embrace the future—and everything in between—these are the sorts of thoughts and questions that Ethan Mollick provokes in this book.

While it could help my grandma become a skilled ChatGPT prompter to refine her lean pork congee recipe, the book's main focus is on offering practical insights and actionable suggestions for developing a healthy relationship with AI in schools and workplaces. Its relevance depends on the degree of occupational skill overlap—so academics and educators may benefit most.

Title: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck: A Counterintuitive Approach to Living a Good Life
Author: Mark Manson
My Review:
While this book can fall under a few genres, the more prominent genre that it falls under is the self help genre. Solely from a self help stand point of view, I believe that this book deserves 4 stars. Personally, I would rate it 3.5 stars, for I am not too fond of self help/non-fiction books in general. Not yet at least.

How appealing this book will be for people depends greatly on their pre-existing experience and knowledge I believe. There are very few ideas that I disagree with in this book, most ideas aren't new to me, but to my surprise, there were a great deal of philosophical and psychological ideas that were new and refreshing to me.

Mark touched on plenty of 'modern day problems' which are relatively new and very much exist. Problems that I personally think are so new that people simply have not come around to curb it. For that reasons, I reckon it's best suited for modern day young adults.

Anyone looking to expand their horizons, or to compare and contrast your current values, I recommend giving this book a read. With some personal stories and humour, Mark makes a bitter yet crucial pill go down easy.

Title: They Both Die at the End (Death-Cast, #1)
Author: Adam Silvera
My Review:
A great book that serves well as a reminder. This book tells you how it will end right off the bat. The joy in reading this book is not finding out what happens at the end, and instead, how things will unfold, which leads to the already-known ending.

It's interesting to read about how the two protagonists reacted to the knowledge of knowing that their death is imminent. I imagine if this was reality; being notified on the day you will pass, people would react in drastically different ways to it. When imagining myself in a similar situation, things that I spend most of my time doing each day suddenly seem so unimportant and trivial, and things that I often take for granted suddenly become all that matters. This thought experiment can really put things and your values into perspective for you. Of course, we cannot and shouldn't divert all of our focus and attention to making the most out of the present while forgetting about the future. Nevertheless, we all must die eventually on a long enough time scale. As the saying that the book constantly reminds me of: "memento mori", which in Latin literally means "remember you must die". Acknowledging and coming to terms with that fact could change your values for the better and make you spend your limited time more wisely.

Overall, I love the idea and concept of the book, but I do think it could have had a better execution. The writing style isn't bad, but I am just not a fan of it. I am glad I picked up this book, and I'm confident that the moral of this story will stay with me.

Title: The Hike
Author: Drew Magary
My Review:
Absolutely love this book! It's paradoxical, twisted, heartwarming, heartbreaking, exciting, foreboding, and so much more.

The odyssey that this book takes you on will greatly expand your imagination and have you absurdly wondering and questioning about your life as you know it. At times it's funny, at times it's gruesome and terrifying, and most of the time it bring about a combination of emotion. The story also have a great mixture of themes which is a characteristic of an adventure, and that made the odyssey more surreal.

I often like to think that you could get a lifetime of experience from reading a book, though not comprehensively, but following along with the protagonist on his journey do gives some insight on some of the wisdom that can be attained on a journey as such. I enjoyed every part of the story, and I would highly recommend it to anyone who reads for pleasure!

Title: Wuthering Heights A Retelling
Author: Tanya Landman
My Review:
To begin with, I have never read the original version. From what I can gather, this retelling of the original is told from a different perspective; Catherine's. It is, I believe more concise, summarized, and simplified. Thus making it a great quick read, especially for those looking to have a grasp on the iconic book without having to spend the time to read the meticulously written original.

That being said, this retelling got me more interested in the original. The simplified 19th century English was new and interesting to me. The turn of events in the plot, and the tragic lives of the majority of the characters made it very captivating. I also enjoyed the themes that it explores; love, passion, power, class, revenge, and obsession. However, I do find it rather dramatic.

To sum it up, I think Tanya did a fabulous job at writing the retelling. I would give her a 5 star for her efforts. It is simple enough for a teenager to read, and intriguing enough for an adult as well.

Title: Individutopia
Author: Joss Sheldon
My Review:
This novel depicts a dystopian future that greatly exaggerate the direction in which our current society is headed. Although it’s possible, but I find the setting and the situation in general very unrealistic. It does however makes it a pretty interesting book to read, and also insightful in the most peculiar way.

I enjoyed how the novel reflected a lot of flaws that humans currently have. I especially enjoyed the sorts of addiction Joss Sheldon imagine people to have in the future because it shares a lot of similarities with a lot of the addictions people face nowadays, and how if left ignored, it can become almost unmanageable and unbearable.

The plot and ending however, could be better. Some character’s motives are really preposterous, and the ending is really tacky. Some elements of the setting are illogical and could have better reasoning behind it.

All in all it’s a pretty interesting novel.

Title: Counting by 7s
Author: Holly Goldberg Sloan
My Review:
A wonderful novel that I wish I would have read at a younger age. The story is humorous, heartfelt, inspiring and has the best possible ending the story could have. I like how Holly was able to euphemistically introduced the notion that life could be messy, unfair, uncertain, and yet worth-while to young readers through her story. It certainly isn't an easy thing to do.

If I were to change something about the story, I would change the protagonist's level of ingenuity. I find it unrealistic for the protagonist to be this precocious this young. However, one could argue that it does not have to be realistic because it could be beneficial for younger readers to believe that the sky's the limit!

With all the reasons above, I think that this book should be read!
